summary: This document updates the changes that RFC 8447 made to the IANA registries for TLS and DTLS. It adds a new value, "D" for discouraged, to the Recommended column of selected registries and adds a Comment column to the active registries that lack one. It also updates the registration requests for these registries.

plainLanguage.summary: There is a big public list of the options that secure connections can use. This adds a way to mark options as "better not to use" and a notes column for explaining why.

subtitle: Adding a way to mark discouraged cryptographic options in TLS registry tables.

tldr.problem: The IANA registries for TLS and DTLS codepoints (cipher suites, algorithms, extensions) only marked items as recommended (Y) or not evaluated (N). There was no way to mark algorithms known to be weak or unsafe.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC adds a new value, D (Discouraged), to the Recommended column of selected registries. It also adds a Comment column to registries that lack one, so weaknesses and conditions can be explained.
tldr.outcome: Implementers can now clearly see which cryptographic options should not be used, and why. The comment columns provide the necessary context to explain why an item is discouraged.

facts.label: Registries affected
facts.value: 13 main registries updated with Recommended column changes

today: RFC 9847 is the current standard for TLS and DTLS IANA registry management. Entries marked D are now the standard way to indicate weak or unsafe cryptographic options that should not be used.

sections.title: The Need for Discouraged Marking
sections.content:
RFC 8447 established IANA registries for all the codepoints that TLS and DTLS (Datagram TLS) use: cipher suites, extensions, supported groups, signature algorithms, and many more. Each entry in these registries had a Recommended column with two values: Y (recommended) or N (not evaluated).

Over time, it became clear that some registered options are not just unevaluated, but actively harmful. NULL encryption provides no secrecy, RC4 is cryptographically broken, DES and MD5 are too weak, and some algorithms like anon (anonymous key exchange) are vulnerable to on-path attacks. These deserved more than an "N" to warn implementers not to use them.
sections.plainLanguage: The menu had checkmarks for safe options, but no way to mark things as dangerous. Now there is a big red X for things that are broken.

sections.title: The Discouraged Value
sections.content:
This RFC adds a third value to the Recommended column: D (Discouraged). An item marked D indicates that the option might result in problems if used, such as a weak cryptographic algorithm or one that causes interoperability issues. When an entry is marked D, either the Reference or Comment column must include sufficient information to explain why.

Setting an entry to D (or changing it from Y or D) requires IETF Standards Action with Expert Review or IESG Approval. This ensures that the marking is made carefully and with proper justification.
sections.plainLanguage: A red X means "do not use this." The next column explains why it is bad.

sections.title: Adding Comment Columns
sections.content:
This RFC also adds a Comment column to all active TLS and DTLS registries that do not already have one. The Comment column allows IANA to record explanations, references, and caveats about each codepoint. For entries marked as Discouraged, the Comment column provides the necessary context for why the item should not be used.

Registries updated with Comment columns include Cipher Suites, Supported Groups, Extension Types, Certificate Types, Hash Algorithms, Signature Algorithms, and many others. The Comment column is left blank for unassigned or reserved entries unless specifically set.
sections.plainLanguage: There is now a notes column next to each option. Next to bad options, it says what is wrong with them.

sections.title: Examples of Discouraged Items
sections.content:
The RFC marks many cipher suites and algorithms as D. NULL encryption cipher suites (those providing no confidentiality) are marked D because protocols and applications typically require confidentiality as a security property. EXPORT cipher suites and anon cipher suites are marked D, as they were deprecated in TLS 1.1. RC4, DES, and IDEA are marked D because they are cryptographically weak. MD5 and SHA-1 are also marked D for hash functions as they are not secure for general use.

For Supported Groups, smaller and weaker elliptic curves such as sect163k1, secp192r1, and secp224r1 are marked D. In the Hash Algorithm registry, md5 and sha1 are marked D. In the Signature Algorithm registry, items are left as N (not evaluated) rather than D, as the RFC notes they have limited applicability or are for specific use cases.
sections.plainLanguage: Broken ciphers like RC4, weak hashes like MD5, and patterns that do not encrypt (NULL) are all marked as "do not use."

sections.title: Expert Review and Registration
sections.content:
The RFC updates the registration procedures for TLS registries. For registries using Specification Required policy, designated experts review and approve new registrations. The RFC clarifies that unless TLS Working Group chairs indicate otherwise, experts should decline registrations for documents already adopted or proposed for adoption by IETF or IRTF working groups.

Registration requests can be submitted by email to iana@iana.org or via the IANA online form. For Specification Required registries, requests are registered after a three-week review period on the advice of one or more designated experts.
sections.plainLanguage: Experts check that new options are ready before they are added to the list. The experts also make sure TLS development inside the IETF and other groups is coordinated.

sections.title: Why This Matters for Security
sections.content:
Cryptographic algorithms and parameters weaken over time as attacks improve. A mechanism marked as recommended today might need to be deprecated later. The Discouraged marking provides a clear, visible way to signal that an option should not be used, helping implementers and users avoid algorithms known to be broken or weak.

The RFC notes that the Recommended status in the registry may lag behind advances in cryptanalysis, so implementers and users must continue to monitor the security status of the algorithms they use. The addition of Comment columns provides room for these updates and explanations.
sections.plainLanguage: Codes that were safe ten years ago might be broken now. The registry now has a way to warn people not to use old or weak codes.

viz.caption: The three values of the Recommended column.

items.label: Recommended
items.desc: The IETF has consensus that the item is fit for its intended purpose.

items.label: Not Evaluated
items.desc: The item has not been evaluated by the IETF, with no statement about its suitability.

items.label: Discouraged
items.desc: The item might result in problems if used; should not be used in general.
